statement: Hwanjile, the kpojito ("queen mother"/reign-mate) of King Tegbesu (r. c.1740-1774), is credited with importing the Mawu-Lisa cult from Aja territory and installing it as head of the Dahomean state pantheon, building it a shrine outside the royal palace and serving as its high priestess. This is treated in the scholarly literature as an act of religious-political legitimation tied to consolidating Tegbesu's contested succession — a datable historical/political act, not static inherited cosmology.

sources.citation: Bay, Edna G. Wives of the Leopard: Gender, Politics, and Culture in the Kingdom of Dahomey. University of Virginia Press, 1998.
sources.author: Edna G. Bay

sources.citation: "Belief, Legitimacy and the Kpojito: An Institutional History of the 'Queen Mother' in Precolonial Dahomey." Journal of African History.
